questions.question:
**Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.**

I am having trouble / deciding in / a gift for them. / no error
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**deciding in**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"deciding in**" in choice 4 **contains a grammar mistake**.
 
• **After "deciding," the proper preposition to use is "on" or "about," not "in."**
 
 
• Example:
 
 
• *I'm having trouble **deciding on **what to order for dinner.*
 
• *She's having a hard time **deciding about **which college to attend.*
 
• *We need to **decide on** a date for the meeting.*
 
 
 
 
 
• In each of these instances, the **word "deciding" is followed by the words "on" or "about," **designating the subject or **choice that the individual is considering.** It would be i**ncorrect to use "in" after "deciding" **since it would confuse the reader.
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 4.**

**Correct Sentence:__ ***I am having trouble __**deciding on**__ a gift for them.*

__
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Let's know more about prepositions:
 
• **Prepositions** are words or phrases that are **used in front of a noun, pronoun**, or noun phrase t**o indicate time, place, location, direction, or spatial relationships, or to present an object.**
 
• A preposition is typically **placed before** the word or phrase it refers to, or** the preposition's object.**
 
• The Preposition should be **followed by an object form of the Pronoun.**
 
 
• Examples: "*in," "at," "on," "of," and "to."*

questions.question:
**Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.**

The company sold the newly introduced car to the highest bidder.

options.text: The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company.
The company sold the newly introduced car to the highest bidder.
The newly introduced car has sold to the highest bidder by the company.
The newly introduced car sold to the highest bidder by the company.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• As we can see the given sentence is in the active voice format of the **simple past tense** as the **second form of the verb (sold)** is applied in the sentence, so we have to **change** the** active** **voice **as per the **same tense rules**.
 
• **Active voice**: Subject +** V2** + object
 
• **Passive voice**: Object + **was/were + V3** + by + subject
 
• Example:
 
 
• Active voice: *Maya **cleaned** the dishes.*
 
• Passive voice: *The dishes** were cleaned by** Maya.*
 
 
 
• By following the above-mentioned rules, we have to change the active to **passive **by applying the** third form of the verb (was sold)** in the **sentence.**

 

**Therefore, the correct answer is**: *The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Let us take a look at the rules of simple past active passive voice:
 
 
• **Active** voice: Subject +** V2** + object
 
• **Passive** voice: Object + **was/were + V3 + by** + subject
 
• **Active** voice: Subject + **did + not + v1 **+ object
 
• **Passive** voice: Object +** was/were + not + V3 + by** Subject
 
• **Active** voice:** Did +** subject + **V1 **+ object +?
 
• **Passive** voice:** Was/were** + Object +** V3 + by** subject +?

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank and complete the collocation.**

Always be in ______ with your near and dear ones as life is uncertain and fragile.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "touch".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **correct collocation is "be in touch".**
 
• Let's understand its meaning:
 
• **Be in touch**__: it refers to **continuing a conversation or point of contact with someone**. Because life can be unpredictable, it's crucial to stay in touch with your loved ones. Doing so can develop bonds and offer emotional support.
 __
 
• Example:
 
 
• *I intentionally try to **be in touch** with my friends and family, even if it's only a quick message or phone call.*
 
• *We need to **be in touch** with the latest trends and technologies if we want our business to stay competitive.*
 
 
 
 
 
• It is apparent from the above explanation that the correct word for the given sentence is** "touch".**

 

Therefore, the complete sentence is: *Always be in **touch**__ with your near and dear ones as life is uncertain and fragile.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• Let's know more about the rest of the options:
 
• The **other possibilities** on the list are also concerned with relationships and communication, but they **don't quite match the sentence's context **as well.
 
• The words **"relation"** and **"connection**" could be used instead, although **"touch" is the most typical collocation**.
 
• The term **"communication" is too general **and **fails to convey the significance **of preserving a long-term relationship.

questions.question:
**Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.**

Professor told me that I could not rescue myself from that bait.

options.text: Professor says to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”
Professor said to me, “You have not rescued yourself from this bait.”
Professor said to us, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”
Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”

questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• As we can see, the indirect speech is in **simple past tense** form (**told, could**), we have to change the **direct speech** according to the **same tense rules.**
 
• **Direct speech**: Subject + **V1st **+ Object
 
• **Indirect speech**: Subject + **V2** + Object
 
 
• Example: Direct speech: *Bhumika Said, “I am a student.”*
 
• Indirect speech:* Bhumika said that she was a student.*
 
 
 
• Consequently, the **same rule** would be applied in the given sentence.
 
• Thus, the **simple past** verb **(could**) would be** changed** to **simple present **tense (**can**).
 
• **'that' **will change into** 'could'.**
 
• **'myself' **will change into** 'yourself'.**
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 4.**

 

**Therefore, the correct answer is:** *Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indirect **communication is referred to as** reporting **the words, but** direct speech** is regarded as **reciting the exact **same words said.
 
• Modals, **reporting verbs, place**, time, tense, pronouns, and other elements all** affect how direct and indirect speech** is changed.
 
• Depending on the subject of the reporting speech, the **first-person pronoun** shifts.
 
• **Eliminate the comma** and the inverted commas, between the reporting and the reported speech, **insert "that."**
 
 
• Example: *Arun Said, “They are in the car.”*
 
• Example: *Arun said that they were in the car.*

• In the English language, **collocation is the regular pairing of two or more words with a frequency greater than chanc**e. It describes a natural **combination of words that are strongly related to one another.**
